description: We're a SL team of 3rd-year SE undergrads passionate about technology, science, AI, and problem-solving. We're looking for an already registered in-person participants who are curious, committed, collaborative, and eager to build a practical, standout solution.
summary: Mihi ("Earth" in Sinhala, මිහි · மிஹி) turns NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar into plain answers about water, land and ground, in Sinhala, Tamil and English. Radar sees through cloud and darkness, so Mihi keeps a "water memory" of where water really stands, pass by pass, for eight areas in four countries; replays Cyclone Ditwah (Nov 2025) against UNESCO's reference flood map with the agreement score on screen; tracks wetland change and fresh land filling; follows paddy seasons, tanks, drought and ground motion; and watches Greenland's fastest glacier beside GRACE ice mass. Anyone can tap a plot for a one-page Plot Passport with a QR code, a read-aloud button and a sound signature, or send a location to a Telegram bot that answers with a voice note. Every layer carries its provenance and its limits, and every test rule was written before the result. Free, open source and live.
details:
The problem: the monsoon blinds the satellites people rely on

Sri Lanka lives by water. Its paddy fields are fed by ancient tank cascades, its cities sit on filled marshland, and twice a year the monsoon brings floods to the lowlands and landslides to the hills. In late November 2025, Cyclone Ditwah brought both at once.

Exactly when it mattered, the sky was full of cloud. Optical satellites, the ones that make the familiar color pictures, cannot see through it, so the flood was only partly visible from space for days. Radar can. The NASA–ISRO NISAR mission now images Sri Lanka every 12 days in L-band, a long radar wavelength (about 24 cm) that passes through cloud, works at night and even reaches water under tree canopies.

But radar images are grey, speckled and hard to read. The people who most need to know where water goes are the least able to read them:

  • Land buyers and valuers cannot tell a filled wetland from solid ground.
  • Farmers, tank committees and insurers cannot see how water behaves across seasons.
  • NGOs and journalists need evidence they can cite, with its source and its limits.
  • Blind, low-vision and low-literacy people get nothing from a map at all.
  • Most Sri Lankans read Sinhala or Tamil first, and almost no Earth-observation tool speaks either.

Our answer: Mihi

Mihi ("Earth" in Sinhala) takes NISAR's radar and turns it into answers a person can act on, in their own language, through whichever door suits them: an interactive map, a one-page report for one plot of land, or a voice note on Telegram.

It works at two speeds:

  • Slow, radar memory. Every 12 days NISAR passes over again. Mihi reads each pass and builds a memory of the land: where water stands, how often, what changed, which fields flood, which tanks fill and drain, whether the ground moves.
  • Fast, rain now and next. Every 30 minutes Mihi refreshes JAXA's satellite rain picture and a 7-day forecast with its spread.
  • Fusion. When rain heads toward a place that radar remembers as water-collecting, Mihi can raise a heads-up for that place.

And it is built on one principle: honesty is a feature. Every number has its dataset, granule IDs, DOI and data maturity one tap away, every method's pass mark was written down before the number was computed, and negative results are shown as they came out. Mihi is a screening tool that points to places worth checking; it is not an official warning service.

Tech Stack

Data access and processing

  • Python 3 pipeline with its own command-line tool (mihi)
  • earthaccess and h5py for reading only the needed window of NISAR HDF5 files over HTTP, never full downloads
  • numpy, scipy, rasterio and GDAL for raster processing
  • scikit-learn for the machine-learning water classifier
  • OpenCV for the Lucas–Kanade optical-flow rain nowcast
  • Google Colab notebooks for heavy jobs

Web app

  • React, TypeScript and Vite
  • MapLibre GL JS with OpenFreeMap base maps and Terrarium 3D terrain
  • three.js with React Three Fiber for the 3D Glacier Lab
  • i18next for Sinhala, Tamil and English
  • Installable offline app (PWA)

Bot and API

  • FastAPI open-data API (GeoJSON, KML, CSV)
  • python-telegram-bot for the Talking Ground bot
  • Text-to-speech: Piper (Sinhala) and Meta MMS (Tamil, English); Opus voice notes

Data storage and hosting

  • Supabase (Postgres with row-level security) for community reports
  • Static Hugging Face Space for the live site, with a Cloudflare Worker for mihi.earth
  • GitHub Actions for automation: rain refresh every 30 minutes, pass list daily, deploy on every merge

Quality

  • pytest (522 tests), vitest, ruff
  • axe-core and Lighthouse for accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA, score 100)
  • An OWASP Top 10 security audit

AI assistance

  • Claude Code (Anthropic), with every session logged in the repository

What you can do with Mihi: the ten lenses

The app is organized as lenses: each one answers a different question about the same ground. A header bar picks the study area, the bottom timeline steps through NISAR passes, and every lens draws its result on the map and explains it in a card.

Lens 1: Water Memory, "where does water come and go?"

What it shows - For each NISAR pass, a map of open water; across all passes, a water-frequency map that colors every 30 m cell by how often it held water (always, seasonally, rarely). A chart gives the water area of each pass, coloured by data maturity (BETA, PROVISIONAL, VALIDATED), and the bottom timeline lets you step through passes and see the radar picture itself under the water colours.

Where - Eight areas in four countries: in Sri Lanka the lower Kelani basin (Colombo), Muthurajawela marsh, the Minneriya tank, northern Polonnaruwa, Kala Wewa and Ampara; abroad Kuttanad (Kerala, India), the braided Jamuna river (Bangladesh) and Padang (Indonesia). That is more than 80 NISAR passes read for real.

How it works

  1. The pass list comes from NASA's Common Metadata Repository (CMR) and refreshes daily.
  2. For each pass, Mihi opens the NISAR L2 GCOV file in the cloud and reads only the window over the study area with HDF5 range requests. For the Kelani basin that is about 150 MB of a 5.6 GB granule (2.7 %). Full granules are never downloaded.
  3. The HH backscatter is despeckled, the sea is removed with a land/sea mask built from ESA WorldCover (keeping lagoons such as Negombo inland), and cells darker than the water threshold (-12 dB) are flagged. Small blobs are removed and gaps closed.
  4. Each pass is also counted inside the area seen on every pass, so passes stay comparable when a radar frame edge moves.
  5. The water-frequency map, the per-pass areas and a provenance record are published to the app.

Built into the lens

  • Tank Pulse: for Minneriya, Polonnaruwa and Kala Wewa, the water area of the tank through the season (Minneriya: 25.3 to 30.7 km² across 12 passes).
  • Independent check against NASA optical water: NISAR water compared with OPERA DSWx-HLS on passes at most one day apart. Overlap (IoU) 0.81 at Muthurajawela (precision 96 %), 0.52 in the Kelani basin.
  • Multi-source confirmation: NISAR and OPERA DSWx-S1 agreeing together reached a confirmed-tier precision of 0.988 against optical water (Ampara).
  • Machine-learning cross-check: a gradient-boosted per-cell classifier trained on NASA optical water labels with spatial-block cross-validation and Kerala fully held out. It beat the threshold at Muthurajawela (IoU 0.891 against 0.816), so it ships as an independent cross-check beside the map.
  • Drought Memory and drought watch: season highest, lowest and latest water; a trend over the last six passes with a 95 % cone ("if the trend continues"); the 90-day rain percentile against 1991–2020 from NASA POWER; a watch level by fixed rules.
  • All areas side by side: every Water Memory area on one chart.
  • Coastal "where to test" map: for Jaffna and Kalpitiya, farmland ranked 0 to 3 by being low-lying, near the sea and near water that comes and goes, as a guide for where to sample well water.

Who it helps - Tank committees, irrigation officers, farmers and anyone asking "does this place hold water, and when?"

Lens 2: Ditwah check, "what did the satellites see during the cyclone?"

What it shows - A replay of Cyclone Ditwah over the Kelani basin, pass by pass, from early November to mid December 2025, with the agreement score against the reference flood map on screen.

How it works

  • Radar track: NASA OPERA RTC-S1 (Sentinel-1) every 12 days through the event, then the one NISAR scene after it (10 Dec 2025). The flood map is "dark now AND at least 3 dB darker than the pre-storm baseline", with the method fixed before any score.
  • Radar + optical view: sixteen NASA OPERA DSWx-HLS optical water maps from Landsat and Sentinel-2 layered in on their dates; cloud is drawn grey as "not observed", never as dry.
  • "What each satellite could see" chart: one mark per pass, its height the share of land actually observed. This is the blind spot made visible: radar passes see everything, optical passes lose the cloudy parts.
  • Water per pass chart: the rise to 2 Dec and the fall after.
  • Score against UNESCO IHP-WINS: precision, recall, F1 and IoU, worded as agreement with a preliminary reference.

What it found - The radar change map on 2 Dec 2025: precision 96 %, recall 12 %. Almost everything radar flags is inside the reference flood, but most of that flood (63 %) lay under trees, where C-band darkness cannot see it. NASA's optical product, on the two clear days, reached recall of 92 % and 59 %, with lower precision because it also counts water that was already there. Showing both, side by side, is the lesson: no single satellite saw the whole flood.

Lens 3: Hidden flood, "can L-band see water under trees?"

What it shows - Where NISAR's L-band HH signal brightened under tree cover after the flood. When water stands under trees, radar bounces off the water surface and then the trunks ("double bounce"), so flooded forest gets brighter, not darker.

How it works - HH change on the NISAR scene of 10 Dec 2025 against a dry-season reference, within tree cover; tested with a spatial-block bootstrap, a shifted-reference null test and a dry-season placebo, all written before the score.

What it found - A real, spatially specific signal: under reference-flooded trees the HH change is +0.55 dB higher than under other trees, beyond every null and placebo, and cells with a 3 dB rise are 2.5 times more likely to be flooded than a random tree cell. Two cross-checks extend it:

  • Against NASA DSWx-HLS: 7,888 radar candidates sorted by what optical saw within 3 days (64 % were in places optical could not observe at all, which is exactly where radar adds value).
  • Against NASA HLS NDVI: the test rerun with three vegetation definitions from HLS greenness.

This is the first step to flood maps that see under the canopy, where the Ditwah radar map missed most of the flood.

Lens 4: Wetland Change, "is the marsh being filled?"

What it shows - For Muthurajawela marsh and the Diyawanna wetlands around Sri Lanka's parliament, how open water has changed since 1984, what the lost water is now, and where radar sees fresh fill.

  • Before/after slider: JRC Global Surface Water (Landsat, 1984 to 2021) on the map. Muthurajawela's open water is stable (33.892 to 34.049 km²); 0.126 km² of lost water is now built-up or bare ground, a short list of candidate places to check.
  • NISAR now: radar water on the latest VALIDATED pass (30.719 km², 30 Oct 2026) shown beside the optical history.
  • Fresh-fill candidates: 30 m cells where NISAR HH stepped up by at least 3 dB and stayed there, beyond a random re-ordering of the passes, with an HLS NDVI check. Diyawanna: 0.026 km² of candidates beyond chance.
  • Land filling over time: a map coloured by the pass from which each cell stayed brighter, and an area-per-pass chart that follows the timeline.
  • Urban encroachment on historical water: of the 1.32 km² that ever held water at Diyawanna, 83 % is still open water and 2.3 % is built-up now.

Who it helps - Land buyers, environmental NGOs, journalists and local authorities. Everything here is worded as a candidate for investigation, never an accusation.

Lens 5: Plot Passport, "tell me about this one piece of land"

What it shows - Tap the map (or type a position) and choose a radius from 50 m to 1 km. Mihi writes a one-page passport for that plot:

  • Open-water history 1984 to 2021 and flags for candidate former open water and candidate filled ground
  • NISAR water frequency (how often radar saw water there)
  • Cyclone Ditwah exposure from the UNESCO reference flood map
  • Land cover now (ESA WorldCover)
  • Slope from NASA's NASADEM (mean and steepest cell, with a class: flat, gentle, moderate, steep)
  • Rain climate from NASA POWER: typical monthly rain and wettest days
  • What each number cannot say, on the same page

Made to be shared and heard

  • QR code that reopens the exact plot, and print / save as PDF on one A4 page
  • Read aloud with the device voice in English, Sinhala or Tamil
  • Sound signature: a 10-second tune of the place's water history (low note, little water; high note, more water), saveable as a WAV file, with a spoken legend first
  • Feel the flags: a vibration pattern by number of screening flags, for people who cannot see the screen
  • Report for review: "this passport looks wrong", "water here", "water gone", "ground cracked"; the place is rounded to about 100 m and nothing shows publicly until a person reviews it
  • Community reports that passed review appear as dots on the map

Where - Six Sri Lankan areas with full grids, and through the bot a simpler world version for any point from 60° S to 80° N.

Lens 6: Rain Now/Next, "where is it raining, and what's coming?"

  • Satellite rain now: JAXA's GSMaP_NOW half-hourly rain picture over Sri Lanka, played as an animation, with the rain rate and share of the area raining.
  • Next 3 hours: a nowcast that moves the rain field with optical flow (Lucas–Kanade motion), scored against "nothing moves" so its skill is on screen.
  • 7-day outlook with its spread: NOAA GFS 31-run ensemble through Open-Meteo, as a 10th to 90th percentile band per day, the share of runs with a heavy day and the share reaching the 75, 100 and 150 mm levels used in landslide warnings in the next 72 hours.
  • Radar freshness clock: the last and next NISAR pass, and the measured delay from pass to product (median 2.2 days in the Kelani basin).

How it stays fresh - A GitHub Actions job pulls the latest frames every 30 minutes and publishes them to the live site; a daily job refreshes the NISAR pass list.

Lens 7: Ground Motion, "is the ground moving?"

  • Radar ground motion: 18 NISAR L2 GUNW interferogram pairs over Matale–Kandy (one ascending and one descending chain of nine), turned into line-of-sight displacement (phase × λ / 4π, λ ≈ 0.24 m) and a velocity map, with a coherence mask, a per-pair noise floor and an ionosphere-corrected variant.
  • Landslide watch: live for Matale–Kandy, Kegalle, Badulla and Nuwara Eliya: the last 24 hours, the next 24 hours and the wettest 24 hours in the next three days, against the 75 / 100 / 150 mm levels reported in NBRO landslide warnings.
  • Corridor Watch: 393 km of main road and 58 km of railway around Badulla, and 117 km and 36 km around Nuwara Eliya, cut into 200 m pieces and flagged for steep ground (NASADEM) and Ditwah landslides nearby. A list of pieces to inspect.
  • Ditwah landslide reference from UNESCO IHP-WINS on the map.

What it found - The provisional pairs have a noise floor of 45 mm/year (ascending) and 292 mm/year (descending), so slow landslide creep is below what this data can resolve today. The pipeline is ready for calibrated pairs as NISAR matures.

Lens 8: Paddy Pulse, "how do the rice fields change?"

What it shows - Around the Minneriya tank, 13.92 km² of cropland followed through 11 NISAR passes: how much each 30 m cell's radar brightness changed through the season, against nearby forest as a control, and checked cell by cell against NASA HLS NDVI greenness from 37 scenes.

What it found - Cropland moves 2.7 dB more than forest, and the cropland average swings 3.3 dB over the season, so radar clearly sees the farming season.

Farmland change over the years - A second card uses 144 HLS scenes to measure the share of Minneriya cropland that was green at every Maha and Yala season peak since 2013/14 (23 seasons), with a trend per season type and season rain as context. It shows which seasons were unusually poor.

Lens 9: Radar View, "show me the radar itself"

  • Every NISAR pass as a picture, on one fixed grey scale, for nine areas: play them as a timeline, swipe-compare any two passes, or download an animated GIF with the date, maturity and attribution on every frame.
  • Blind spots: places at least 1 km from any mapped road, path or railway where radar saw change, ranked with fly-to buttons. These are the places nobody visits, and radar watches them every 12 days.
  • Asia readiness atlas: live NASA CMR counts for 22 flood-prone rivers, deltas and cities across South and Southeast Asia. Every one already has 22 to 126 NISAR GCOV scenes, 9 of them with a pass in the last 3 days. The same pipeline runs there today.

Lens 10: ICE2OCEAN, "from glacier motion to global sea level"

An extension that takes the same radar engine to Greenland.

  • 3D Glacier Lab: NISAR feature tracking between 27 Sep and 9 Oct 2026 over Jakobshavn Isbræ, one of Greenland's fastest glaciers: 8,227 of 8,896 grid points valid, fastest 49.3 m/day, shown flat or in 3D on the terrain, with a text table of the same values for screen readers.
  • Validation Lab: against the ITS_LIVE velocity mosaic, the pattern correlates at r = 0.903 over 6,544 points (MAE 5.49 m/day, bias +0.18 m/day), and stable bedrock reads a median of 0.06 m/day.
  • Ice-Mass Timeline: JPL GRACE / GRACE-FO Greenland mass since 2002, with uncertainty. Our refit trend is -258.99 Gt/yr, matching the published value.
  • Ocean-Level Simulator: 6,086 ± 158 Gt lost from April 2002 to September 2026, which is 16.91 ± 0.44 mm of global sea-level rise.
  • Evidence Chain: how each number links to its source. Glacier speed is never converted into sea level; the two are shown side by side as complementary evidence.

Across the whole app

Provenance on every layer, and "How sure are we?"

  • Provenance panel: for the pass on the timeline, the real granule IDs, collection, maturity and DOI. Every published layer has a provenance record with dataset, collection, granule IDs, DOI, maturity and the code version that made it.
  • Trust badge on every card (Cross-checked / Several sources / One source) that opens the single "How sure are we?" page: multi-source cross-check scores, every source and limit per feature, data maturity levels, credits and a privacy statement.
  • Attribution on every map: "Contains NISAR data (NASA–ISRO, ASF DAAC)" plus each layer's own source.

Talking Ground: the Telegram bot

For people who will never open a map. Share a location (or type a place name or coordinates) and the bot answers with:

  • a voice note in Sinhala, Tamil or English, made of whole spoken sentences (no digits to mishear), ready in under 2 seconds once warm,
  • a text card with the exact numbers,
  • the 10-second sound signature of the place,
  • Watch this place: a heads-up when forecast rain heads toward a place radar remembers as water-collecting (rain alone never fires it),
  • Report what you see here: four tap-to-send report kinds, place rounded to about 100 m, no photos, voice or free text stored.

Every AI voice is labelled as AI-generated in its caption and file metadata.

Guided tour

One button (Tour) runs an 11-step, 4-minute story that drives the app's own controls: the blind spot, the Ditwah agreement, Radar View through the season, Muthurajawela, a Plot Passport, hearing it, ground motion and Corridor Watch, the 3D Glacier Lab, GRACE ice mass and sea level, and the limits. Back, Pause, Next, Exit and a captions on/off switch.

Warning Centre

A Watch button in the header with a count of active watches: the live landslide rain watch for the four hill districts and the drought watch for the Water Memory areas, each linking into its lens.

Accessibility, built in from day one

  • WCAG 2.2 AA: axe-core 0 violations on every lens in English, Sinhala and Tamil, at phone width, in larger-text mode and with dialogs open; Lighthouse accessibility 100.
  • Skip link, landmarks, page language that follows the chosen language, translated labels, keyboard-friendly dialogs, larger text (A+), reduced motion honored, large touch targets, color-blind-safe map keys, text tables beside charts.
  • Sound, vibration and voice as alternatives to sight.

Three languages, light and dark, 3D, offline

  • Sinhala, Tamil and English everywhere.
  • Light and dark mode that follows the device and swaps the base map.
  • 3D terrain toggle.
  • Installable app that works offline with the last view cached.
  • User guide that explains every lens (what, how, data, limits) in all three languages.

Open data and API

An open API serves study areas as GeoJSON, KML and CSV, the real NISAR pass list, Plot Passport grid cells and a plot answer for any point, with interactive documentation and an attribution header on every response.

Anywhere on Earth

Any rectangle up to 2 × 2 degrees can be registered and processed with the same pipeline, and a Google Colab notebook lets anyone run their own area.

How it works

  • Data in: NASA Earthdata (NISAR GCOV and GUNW, OPERA DSWx-HLS, DSWx-S1 and RTC-S1, HLS, NASADEM, NASA POWER, GRACE/GRACE-FO, ITS_LIVE, CMR) plus JAXA GSMaP_NOW, NOAA GFS, ESA WorldCover, JRC Global Surface Water and UNESCO IHP-WINS.
  • Pipeline: a Python package and command line tool (mihi) with one command per feature. It reads NISAR windows straight from NASA's cloud with earthaccess and h5py range reads, resumes and retries on a slow link, reads each file's projection from the file, and never falls back to a full download. Heavy jobs have Colab notebooks.
  • Outputs: small JSON and PNG results, each with its provenance record, published to the web app and the open API.
  • Web app: React, TypeScript and MapLibre GL, with three.js for the 3D Glacier Lab and three languages; each lens and the map load on demand.
  • Bot: FastAPI and python-telegram-bot with open text-to-speech models.
  • Automation and hosting: GitHub Actions refresh rain every 30 minutes, the pass list daily, and redeploy the site on every merge, to a free static Hugging Face Space fronted by mihi.earth. Community reports go to Supabase with row-level security. Everything runs on free tiers.
  • Quality: over 500 Python tests plus web tests run on every change, and an OWASP Top 10 security audit with all findings fixed.

Science methods

  • Open water: HH below -12 dB after despeckling, blob removal and a land/sea mask.
  • Flood: dark now AND at least 3 dB darker than the pre-event baseline.
  • Flooded vegetation: HH rise of at least 3 dB under tree cover or NDVI ≥ 0.4 (L-band double bounce).
  • Fresh fill: a steady HH step of at least 3 dB on wet cells, beyond a permuted-order null, with an NDVI check.
  • Ground motion: GUNW phase to line-of-sight displacement = phase × λ / 4π, masking coherence below 0.4.
  • Glacier motion: normalised cross-correlation feature tracking on a 240 m grid.
  • Rain nowcast: Lucas–Kanade optical flow on GSMaP_NOW frames, scored against persistence.

Validation, pre-registered - Every test, its reference and its pass mark were written down and committed before the number was computed; any change afterwards is recorded as a dated amendment. References include UNESCO IHP-WINS, NASA OPERA DSWx-HLS and DSWx-S1, DIST-ALERT, ERA5, NASA POWER, the NASA Global Landslide Catalog, ITS_LIVE and GRACE.

Benefits and impact

  • Sees when others are blind. Radar memory works through monsoon cloud, at night, and partly under trees.
  • Meets people where they are. A map for analysts, one page for a land buyer, a voice note for a farmer, sound and vibration for a blind user, in Sinhala, Tamil or English.
  • Makes NISAR usable today. Window reads mean a laptop on a slow link can use a 5.6 GB granule; the Asia atlas shows 22 flood-prone places already have the data.
  • Builds trust by showing its work. Provenance, pre-registered tests and published negative results give NGOs, journalists and agencies something they can cite.
  • Costs nothing to run or reuse. Free tiers, MIT-licensed code, open data API.

Who benefits - Land buyers and valuers, farmers and tank committees, insurers, disaster NGOs, journalists, local authorities, visually impaired and low-literacy people, and researchers anywhere NISAR passes.

What makes it creative

  • Radar you can hear - The sound signature turns a place's water history into a melody and its screening flags into vibration.
  • Water memory, not water snapshots - Every pass adds to what the ground remembers.
  • Two-speed fusion - Slow radar memory meets fast rain to say which places matter when rain comes.
  • Honesty as a design element - Amber is reserved for limits so a caution is never decoration; trust badges, a "How sure are we?" page and pre-registered rules are part of the product, not an appendix.
  • From a Sri Lankan plot to Greenland's ice - One engine, from a 100 m plot passport to global sea level.

What we considered

  • Data access on a constrained machine: never download full granules; window reads, resumable stacks, Colab for heavy jobs.
  • Data maturity: BETA, PROVISIONAL and VALIDATED NISAR passes are labelled on every chart and timeline.
  • Language and literacy: three languages, spoken sentences without digits, read-aloud and sound.
  • Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA from the first commit, audited with axe-core and Lighthouse.
  • Privacy: no analytics or cookies; reports rounded to about 100 m; no photos, voice or free text stored from the bot; nothing public until reviewed.
  • Responsible wording: "screening", "candidate", "possible", "for investigation"; never "predicts".
  • Limits, stated once and clearly: radar finds open water well but most of the Ditwah flood was under trees; the L-band under-canopy signal is promising but not yet a detector; the provisional ground-motion pairs are too noisy for slow creep; the rain nowcast matches but does not beat persistence; Sinhala and Tamil text is machine-drafted and awaiting native review. These are the next steps, and all are on the "How sure are we?" page.

What's next

  • SWOT water levels to turn tank area into volume
  • DSWx labels across Asia to train and validate the water model beyond Sri Lanka
  • Calibrated GUNW with tropospheric correction for landslide creep
  • Native-speaker review of Sinhala and Tamil, then the bot on a free host for everyone
  • Partnerships with Sri Lanka's NBRO, the Irrigation Department and disaster NGOs
